slides.title: The whole machine on one screen
slides.summary: An LLM takes a list of numbers (tokens) and gives a score to every possible next token. The rest of this course explains how.
body: The Assistant architecture section treated the model as one box in a bigger system. This section opens that box.

Take away the chat window and a large language model is one huge maths function. You give it a list of whole numbers, one for each piece of text. It gives back a score for every token it knows, showing how likely each one is to come next.
That's all it does. <mark>To write a whole answer, it runs this function again and again, adding one token each time.</mark> The next slide shows that loop.

Each stage on the right turns one block of numbers into another. A block of numbers with several dimensions is called a tensor, and its shape lists how big each dimension is. Following the shapes is the quickest way to understand how the model works. Four letters come up everywhere:

ul: B, batch size: how many separate texts are handled at once.
n, sequence length: how many tokens are in each text.
d, model width: how many numbers describe each token. Usually 4,096 or more.
V, vocabulary size: how many different tokens the model knows. Often 100,000 or more.

body.note: Think of a tensor of shape [B, n, d] as number[][][] in TypeScript: B texts, each with n tokens, each token a list of d numbers. Libraries store it as one flat array for speed, but this is a good way to picture it.

body: Click a stage on the right to jump to its chapter.
code: for block in blocks:          # N times

viz.html: Typical sizes: d = 4,096, N = 32 layers, V = 128,000. When generating, only the scores for the last token matter.

figure.alt: Text is split into token IDs, each ID becomes a vector of d numbers, the vectors flow through N transformer blocks, and the final layer gives a score for every vocabulary token. Softmax turns the last position's scores into probabilities, one token is picked, appended to the text, and the whole pass runs again.
figure.caption: The whole model on one page. Follow the shapes: [n] → [n, d] → [n, V]. Numbers are illustrative.

slides.title: Generation is a loop
slides.summary: The model only ever predicts one token. Long answers come from running it in a loop and feeding each prediction back in.
body: The model can't write a sentence in one go. It predicts just the next token. The program adds that token to the input, and the model runs again on the longer text. This is called autoregressive decoding: each output becomes part of the next input.
Press Run one step to watch it happen. Each step reads everything so far.

body.h: Two stages, with very different costs

ul: Prefill: first the whole prompt is processed, all its tokens at the same time. GPUs are great at doing lots of maths at once, so the limit here is pure calculation speed (compute-bound). It's the short pause before the first word appears.

Decode: after that, every new token needs its own run through the whole model. Each run does little maths but has to read billions of weights from GPU memory, so the limit is how fast memory can be read (memory-bound). It's the steady word-by-word typing you see. The KV cache (see Output & inference) exists to make this stage cheaper.
Stopping: the loop ends when the model writes a special "end" token, or when the app's length limit is reached.

body.note: Everything an LLM writes, including code, step-by-step reasoning and tool calls, <mark>comes out of this loop one token at a time</mark>.

code: logits = model(ids)[-1]        # only the last position

steps.caption: Just the prompt. Step 1 processes all 3 tokens at once (prefill).
Run 2 done. The text is now 4 tokens long; the model reads it all again (or reuses its cache).

slides.title: Vectors and similarity: the maths you need
slides.summary: Almost everything inside an LLM is a list of numbers, called a vector. The most important operation is measuring how similar two vectors are.
body: You need very little maths for this course. These three ideas cover most of it.

body.h: 1. A vector is a list of numbers

body: Pick a few features and you can describe anything with numbers. Describe fruit by [sweetness, crunchiness, sourness], each from 0 to 1, and an apple might be [0.7, 0.9, 0.3]. That list is a vector, and each slot is a dimension.
To get the dot product of two vectors, multiply them slot by slot and add up the results. It's big when both vectors are big in the same places, so it works as a similarity score.

Cosine similarity is the dot product adjusted for each vector's length, so only the direction counts, not the size. It goes from −1 (opposite) through 0 (unrelated) to 1 (same direction). Try different pairs on the right.

body.h: 3. A matrix multiply is many dot products at once

body: A matrix is a grid of numbers. Multiplying a vector by a matrix does one dot product per column and gives a new vector. A neural network is mostly long chains of these multiplications, and the numbers in the matrices are learned from data.

body.note: An LLM describes every token with a vector of thousands of numbers. Nobody decides what those dimensions mean, like we did for fruit; training works them out. But <mark>the key idea, that similar meanings have similar vectors, runs through the whole course</mark>.

code: return sum(x * y for x, y in zip(a, b))
return dot(a, b) / (norm(a) * norm(b))   # norm = length

slides.title: A short glossary
slides.summary: The few words that come up on almost every slide.
body: Each term is explained fully the first time it matters. Come back to this list if a word on a later slide feels unfamiliar.
Two ideas matter more than any single definition:

ul: Everything is numbers. Text becomes whole numbers, those become vectors, and the model just does maths on the vectors.

Behaviour comes from learned numbers. Nobody writes an LLM's knowledge or style by hand. Billions of numbers are adjusted during training until the model predicts text well, and everything it can do comes from those numbers.

body.note: A handy comparison with software: training is like a very long, very expensive build that produces a file (the weights). Inference is running that file. Most of this course is about inference; the Training chapter covers the build.

items.label: Token
items.sub: A piece of text: a word, part of a word, or a symbol.

items.label: Vocabulary
items.sub: The fixed list of every token the model knows, each with a number as its ID.

items.label: Vector / tensor
items.sub: A list of numbers / a block of numbers with several dimensions.

items.label: Embedding
items.sub: The vector that represents one token inside the model.

items.label: Parameter (weight)
items.sub: One learned number inside the model. Model sizes count these.

items.label: Layer (block)
items.sub: One repeated unit of the model: attention, then an MLP (a small neural network).

items.label: Forward pass
items.sub: One run of the model, from token IDs in to scores out.

items.label: Logit
items.sub: The raw score the model gives each possible next token.

items.label: Softmax
items.sub: Turns a list of scores into probabilities that add up to 1.

items.label: Hallucination
items.sub: Fluent, confident text that isn't true.

items.label: Training / inference
items.sub: Learning the parameters / using them to generate text.
